detailed_summary: This paper addresses the long-standing question of whether a three-dimensional quantum many-body system with geometrically local, bounded-degree interactions can passively protect quantum information against both thermal noise and static Hamiltonian perturbations. Building on the recent work of Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (BDL), who introduced a recursively defined family of stabilizer Hamiltonians achieving thermal self-correction in the unperturbed case, the authors propose a slight variant of the BDL code family and prove its stability along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram as system size grows. Specifically, they show that in the absence of perturbations, the system is thermally stable below a critical temperature, exhibiting a stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime when coupled to any local Markovian thermal bath satisfying detailed balance. At zero temperature, under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, the family maintains a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables. The proof of zero-temperature stability relies on establishing local topological quantum order across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria. In a companion paper, the authors combine these tools with finite-temperature worldline cluster expansions to establish passive self-correction throughout the positive-temperature perturbed interior of the phase diagram. This work represents a significant step toward realizing robust topological quantum memories in three dimensions.
key_contributions: Introduces a variant of the BDL stabilizer code family that achieves stability against both thermal noise and static perturbations in three dimensions.

Proves zero-temperature stability under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, including a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables.

Establishes local topological quantum order across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria, a novel technique for analyzing perturbed topological codes.
Demonstrates thermal stability below a critical temperature with a stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime when coupled to any local Markovian thermal bath satisfying detailed balance.
Together with a companion paper, provides a comprehensive proof of passive self-correction throughout the positive-temperature perturbed interior of the phase diagram.
methodology_analysis: The authors employ a rigorous mathematical physics approach combining stabilizer code theory, perturbation theory, and statistical mechanics. They start from the BDL recursive code family, which is built on a hierarchical structure of concatenated toric codes, and modify it to enhance robustness. The zero-temperature stability proof hinges on establishing a local topological quantum order (LTQO) condition across the multiscale hierarchy. To achieve this, they develop a 'linearly dilated relaxation' of the Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis (BHM) criteria, which are standard tools for proving stability of topological phases. This relaxation allows them to handle the recursive structure and the presence of perturbations that decay superpolynomially with distance. The thermal stability analysis uses a combination of detailed balance arguments and cluster expansion techniques to bound the memory lifetime. The companion paper extends these methods to finite temperature using worldline cluster expansions, providing a unified framework for analyzing the entire phase diagram.
results_analysis: The key results are twofold: at zero temperature, the system exhibits a uniform bulk spectral gap that is stable under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying perturbations. The ground-space splitting is superpolynomially small, and the closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables is superpolynomially long. These results hold for any perturbation that decays faster than any polynomial, a very general class. At finite temperature, below a critical temperature, the memory lifetime is stretched-exponentially long when coupled to a local Markovian bath. The stretched-exponential scaling, while not as strong as exponential, still represents a significant improvement over previous results and is sufficient for passive protection in many practical scenarios. The authors do not provide explicit numerical values for the critical temperature or the exponents, as the proofs are asymptotic and focus on scaling with system size. However, the results are rigorous and establish the existence of a stable phase.
strengths: Provides a rigorous proof of stability against both thermal and static perturbations for a 3D topological code family, addressing a major open problem.
Introduces a novel technique (linearly dilated relaxation of BHM criteria) that may be applicable to other hierarchical topological codes.
The results are robust, holding for arbitrary weak perturbations with superpolynomial decay, which is a very general and physically relevant class.
The work is part of a larger effort (with a companion paper) that covers the entire phase diagram, demonstrating comprehensive analysis.
limitations: The memory lifetime at finite temperature is only stretched-exponential, not exponential, which may limit practical applications for very long storage times.
The analysis assumes a specific local Markovian thermal bath satisfying detailed balance; more general baths or non-Markovian effects are not considered.
The construction is a variant of the BDL code, which is highly complex and may be challenging to implement experimentally due to its recursive structure and required precision in interactions.
connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly in the areas of topological quantum computation, quantum error correction, and many-body physics. It addresses fundamental questions about the stability of quantum information in the presence of noise and perturbations, which is crucial for building scalable quantum computers. The techniques developed, such as the linearly dilated relaxation of BHM criteria, are of interest to researchers studying topological phases and their robustness. The results also have implications for understanding self-correcting quantum memories and the phase diagram of quantum systems with local interactions.
overall_assessment: This paper represents a significant theoretical advance in the quest for passively protected quantum memories in three dimensions. It provides rigorous proofs of stability against both thermal and static perturbations for a specific code family, overcoming a major hurdle that has hindered progress in the field. The novelty lies in the construction of the variant code and the development of new mathematical tools for analyzing perturbed topological order. While the finite-temperature lifetime is only stretched-exponential and the code is complex, the work is of high quality and will likely stimulate further research in topological quantum computation and statistical mechanics. It is a valuable contribution to the literature and a must-read for researchers interested in quantum error correction and topological phases.
